section.title: Pleasure and Toil Are Fleeting
section.sectionRationale: The great experiment. The Teacher pours his royal wealth and wisdom into every pleasure, project, and possession a person could want, then weighs the result. He finds that pleasure, achievement, and even wisdom all run aground on the same rock: death levels the wise and the fool alike, and everything a person builds must be left to someone else. Yet the chapter does not end in the dark. It turns, for the first time, to God, whose hand gives food, work, and joy as gifts.
section.thesis: The Teacher tests pleasure, achievement, wisdom, and toil to their limits and finds each one hevel, a fleeting breath, because death and loss undo them all; yet the chapter turns at its close to the God from whose hand ordinary food, work, and joy come as gifts to those who please Him.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the test of pleasure; the great works and wealth; the wise and the fool who share one fate; the toil that must be left to another; and the turn upward, food, work, and joy from the hand of God.

units.label: The test of pleasure
units.note: come now, enjoy what is good

verses.text: I said to myself, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!” But it proved to be {{hevel|futile}}.
I said of laughter, “It is folly,” and of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?”
I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly, my mind still guiding me with wisdom, until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.
I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself.
I made gardens and parks for myself, where I planted all kinds of fruit trees.
I built reservoirs to water my groves of flourishing trees.
I acquired menservants and maidservants, and servants were born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me,
and I accumulated for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I gathered to myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men, many concubines.
So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.
Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my {{amal|labor}}.

Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the {{ruach|wind}}; there was nothing to be {{yitron|gained}} under the sun.

units.label: One fate for the wise and the fool
units.note: the wise man dies just like the fool

verses.text: Then I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly; for what more can the king’s successor do than what has already been accomplished?
And I saw that {{chokmah|wisdom}} exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness:
The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both.
So I said to myself, “The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?” And I said to myself that this too is futile.
For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come. Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!
So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind.

units.label: The toil left to another
units.note: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verses.text: I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish? Yet he will take over all the labor at which I have worked skillfully under the sun. This too is futile.
So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun.
When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great evil.
For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun?
Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile.

units.label: Gifts from the hand of God

verses.text: Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.
For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?

To the man who is pleasing in His sight, He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.

hevel.gloss: Literally vapor or breath, the keyword of Ecclesiastes, translated futility, meaningless, or fleeting. Pleasure, achievement, wisdom, and toil are each pronounced hevel: real and even good, yet slipping through the fingers like a breath, unable to bear the weight of ultimate hope.

amal.gloss: Toil, laborious work, and the trouble that comes with it. It runs through this chapter as the Teacher surveys everything his hands built, all the burdened labor that fills the days and must, in the end, be handed over to someone else.

yitron.gloss: Gain, profit, advantage, the surplus left when the accounts are settled. After the greatest building program and pleasure quest imaginable, the Teacher totals the ledger and finds there was nothing to be gained under the sun.

ruach.gloss: Wind, breath, or spirit. In the recurring phrase a pursuit of the wind it pictures striving to grasp or herd the breeze: exhausting effort that closes on nothing, the Teacher's verdict on pleasure, achievement, and toil alike.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of living well. The Teacher affirms that wisdom truly exceeds folly as light exceeds darkness, yet even the wise share the fool's fate in death, so wisdom, good as it is, cannot finally rescue from the grave.

basic.context: This chapter is the Teacher's great experiment. Using his unlimited royal resources, he throws himself into everything a person might chase for happiness: wine and laughter, grand houses and gardens, herds and flocks, silver and gold, singers and every desire his eyes fixed on. He holds nothing back. He also keeps his wisdom through it all, so this is no reckless binge but a controlled test. Then he weighs the results. Pleasure did not satisfy. His great achievements felt empty, because he must leave them all to whoever comes after him, wise or foolish. And death lies at the end of it for the wise man and the fool alike. But then the chapter turns. For the first time it lifts its eyes to God, and finds that the simple gifts of food, drink, work, and joy come from His hand.
basic.hermeneutics: Two things hold this chapter together. First, the refrain hevel, a breath: everything the Teacher tests is real and some of it is genuinely good, but none of it lasts or delivers ultimate profit, because death undoes it and someone else inherits it. Second, the turn in verses 24 to 26. This is not a grudging shrug but the book's first ray of light: ordinary joys, received from God's hand as gifts rather than seized as wages, are the good God gives. Read the darkness honestly, and let the turn upward be genuinely good news.
basic.originalLanguages: The word hevel, breath, is stamped on pleasure, work, and toil throughout. The Teacher's building and gathering are his amal, his toil, and when he totals the account he finds no yitron, no lasting profit, under the sun; the effort was a pursuit of the ruach, the wind. He grants that chokmah, wisdom, truly exceeds folly as light exceeds darkness, yet even the wise die. The relief comes only when a new word enters the frame: God, from whose hand food, work, and joy are given.
basic.typology: The Teacher, a son of David who gains the whole world and finds it cannot satisfy, is a shadow that sets off the true Son of David. Where Solomon amasses everything and leaves it to an unknown heir, Christ owns all things, lays down His life, and secures an inheritance that cannot perish for His people. And the simple bread and cup received as gifts from God's hand foreshadow the table where Christ gives Himself as the true food and drink.
basic.christ: Jesus is the greater than Solomon who refuses the shortcut of gaining the whole world, for what does it profit a man to gain the world and forfeit his soul, Mark 8:36. He enters the futility and the grave that level the wise and the fool, and rises, so that our labor is not in vain in the Lord, 1 Corinthians 15:58. The gift of food, work, and joy from God's hand is deepened at His table, where He gives His own body and blood, the bread of life that death cannot take away.
basic.god: For the first time in the book God is named as giver. He is the one from whose hand ordinary joys come, and He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please Him. The lesson is not that pleasure is bad but that it can only be received rightly as a gift, never seized as a wage. Life closed off under the sun is a breath; life opened upward to the God who gives becomes daily grace.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 10 records Solomon's staggering wealth, the very abundance tested here. Mark 8:36 asks what it profits to gain the world and lose the soul. Luke 12 tells of the rich fool who stores up treasure and must leave it behind. 1 Corinthians 15:58 promises that labor in the Lord is not in vain.
basic.oneStory: The richest, wisest king tries every path to lasting satisfaction and finds them all a breath, undone by death and loss. Yet the chapter turns from the emptiness of grasping to the goodness of receiving, naming God as the giver of daily bread, work, and joy. That turn is the Bible in miniature: what we cannot secure by seizing, God gives by grace, and gives fully in Christ, the greater than Solomon who makes even our fleeting labor last forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 2 is written as a royal memoir, and its grammar gives the game away. In verses 4 to 10 nearly every clause is first person and reflexive: houses and vineyards 'for myself,' gardens 'for myself,' silver and gold 'for myself,' singers 'to myself.' The king is the subject of every verb and the beneficiary of every result. God is not named once until verse 24. The silence is part of the design, because the experiment is run in a world with the Giver deleted.

The chapter falls into four movements. Verses 1 to 11 test pleasure and achievement and end in a verdict. Verses 12 to 17 turn to wisdom itself and meet the leveling fact of death. Verses 18 to 23 follow the labor past the grave to an unknown heir. Verses 24 to 26 break the pattern with a statement about the hand of God. The refrain 'this too is futile' sounds eight times in the BSB (verses 1, 11, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23, 26), and it even closes the final verse, which means the light of verses 24 to 26 is set inside the book's gloom, not outside it.

There is a deliberate echo of Eden. The king plants gardens and parks with every kind of fruit tree and digs pools to water them, Ecclesiastes 2:5-6, just as the LORD God planted a garden and sent a river to water it, Genesis 2:8-10. He is a gardener-king who rebuilds paradise by his own hand. Yet the toil of verse 22 is exactly the toil that Genesis 3:17-19 laid on the ground, and no garden he plants can lift it.

The movement from 'I' to 'He' in verse 24 is the hinge of the whole chapter. After twenty-three verses of what the king did, the text turns to what God gives.
context.historical:
The Teacher presents himself as 'the son of David, king in Jerusalem,' Ecclesiastes 1:1, and the experiment in this chapter is cut to the measure of Solomon as 1 Kings describes him. Provisions for a single day at his table ran to flour, oxen, sheep and game, 1 Kings 4:22-23. He spent thirteen years on his own palace, 1 Kings 7:1. Gold flowed in by the talent, his drinking cups were gold, and silver was 'accounted as nothing,' 1 Kings 10:14-21. God had promised him wisdom, and riches and honor besides, 1 Kings 3:12-13. The Teacher's 'I surpassed all in Jerusalem who preceded me,' Ecclesiastes 2:9, borrows that very language.

The tragic irony is that the king broke the Torah's own limits on kingship. Deuteronomy 17:16-17 told Israel's king not to multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold, lest his heart go astray, and 1 Kings 11:1-8 records how it did. When verse 8 lists silver, gold and 'many concubines,' an Israelite reader would feel the weight of that law pressing on the page.

Some details fit a later setting. The word for 'parks' in verse 5, pardes, is a Persian loanword that appears only in Ecclesiastes 2:5, Song of Songs 4:13 and Nehemiah 2:8, and many scholars take the book's language and its use of the word for 'provinces' in verse 8 as marks of a later date than Solomon. Others hold that a royal court with international ties could have used such words early. Either way, the persona is Solomon-like, and the book asks to be read through his story.

Two parallels from the wider world help. Slaves 'born in my house,' verse 7, were a standard mark of a great estate, as with Abram's household-born men in Genesis 14:14. And advice to eat, drink, and enjoy a spouse in the face of death has a close cousin in the tavern-keeper's counsel to Gilgamesh and in Egyptian harpers' songs. Ecclesiastes shares the instinct but roots it in God's gift rather than in resignation.
context.canonical:
This chapter has a dense web of connections. Backward, it reads the curse of Genesis 3:17-19 from the inside: 'through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life' becomes the Teacher's lament that 'all his days are filled with grief,' verse 23. Forward, the two ideas of this chapter, the emptiness of grasping and the goodness of receiving, are developed in the rest of the book: 'this is his lot,' 5:18-20; the rich man who cannot enjoy what he has, 6:1-2; 'eat your bread with joy,' 9:7-10.

The Psalms and Wisdom books supply the same two notes. Psalm 49:16-20 warns that the rich man 'will carry nothing away' and shares the beasts' end, and Psalm 39:6 describes a man who 'heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away,' which is verse 18 almost word for word in idea. Psalm 127:1-2 says toil without the LORD is in vain, 'for He gives sleep to His beloved,' answering the sleepless nights of verse 23. Proverbs 10:22 insists that 'the blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it.'

The prophets look to a time when this curse is lifted: 'they will not labor in vain,' Isaiah 65:21-23, and God invites those who spend their labor 'on that which does not satisfy' to come and eat what is good, Isaiah 55:2.

In the New Testament Paul names the Teacher's word for the world as it is: creation 'was subjected to futility,' Romans 8:20, using the Greek word, mataiotes, that the Septuagint regularly uses for hevel. Jesus tells of the farmer who builds bigger barns and loses his life that night, Luke 12:13-21, and asks what profit is in gaining the whole world, Mark 8:36. Paul counts his own gains as loss, Philippians 3:7-8, and warns Timothy about the love of money, 1 Timothy 6:6-10, while also saying that God 'richly provides all things for us to enjoy,' 1 Timothy 6:17, which is verse 24 in apostolic form.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his listeners to stop trusting the things that most reliably promise life. He does it by letting them watch a man who can afford to test every promise and has no reason to lie about the results. A poor person can always say that wealth would have fixed it. A king who has had it all cannot be answered that way. The experiment closes the escape hatch.

He also wants to loosen the grip of the contest for lasting remembrance. Wisdom, labor and legacy are the hopes of the serious person, and the Teacher shows even those meeting the same wall. The point is not to make his hearers lazy. It is to relocate their security.

Then, with the pivot of verses 24 to 26, he points them to something they can actually do: receive. Eating, drinking, work and joy are to be taken from God's hand, with gratitude, and held loosely. The call is to a posture, not a program. Hearers are meant to leave unable to treat any possession, achievement or pleasure as a savior, and unable to despise any of them as a gift.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first twenty-three verses are the Teacher's report of what he did and felt, not a pattern to copy. Nothing in the text endorses chasing every desire, building a harem or hoarding silver. Deuteronomy 17:17 and 1 Kings 11:1-8 stand in the background as judges of that conduct. Nor is the Teacher's hatred of life in verse 17 a recommended attitude; it is an honest record of where his experiment led, and elsewhere the book tells hearers to rejoice in life, 9:7-9.

What the passage does prescribe is found in verses 24 to 26, and even there the wording is cautious: 'nothing is better,' and 'this is from the hand of God.' It does not command indulgence. It commends receiving ordinary good things with thanks, and it keeps verse 26's moral distinction in view. The believer today can take from this chapter a freedom to enjoy food, work and company without guilt, and a warning against asking any of them to carry weight only God can bear.

debates.question: What does verse 26 teach about who receives joy and who is left gathering?

views.label: A fixed divine sorting
views.case: God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to those who please Him and assigns the sinner the burden of gathering for someone else. Read strictly, this makes God's favor and the gift of enjoyment a matter of His sovereign pleasure, with the verb 'gives' and 'assigns' in His hands.

views.label: Ordinary moral retribution
views.case: The verse mirrors the wisdom tradition: those who live in the fear of God find that life's good things become gifts, while those who live for gain find their gains pass to others, as in Proverbs 13:22 and Job 27:16-17. It is a general pattern, not a promise for every case.

views.label: A bitter irony in the book's own terms
views.case: Because the verse ends with 'this too is futile,' some take it as a comment on the whole puzzle: even God's apparent sorting of people does not remove the mystery. The Teacher notes elsewhere that the righteous and the wicked do not always get what they deserve, Ecclesiastes 7:15.

debates.bearing: The verse does not say that wealth marks God's favor, and the whole book fights that idea. What it does hold fast is that joy is a gift, not a wage. A reader can accept the general pattern of Proverbs while keeping the Teacher's refusal to treat it as a formula.

debates.question: Is verse 24 a call to enjoy life, or a sigh of resignation?

views.label: A shrug in a meaningless world
views.case: Some read the 'nothing is better' sentences across the book as the best a person can do when nothing lasts, close to the carpe diem of other ancient literature. The enjoyment is a distraction from the abyss.

views.label: A confident affirmation of creation's goods
views.case: Others stress 'from the hand of God' in 2:24, 'the gift of God' in 3:13, and 'God has already approved your works' in 9:7. On this reading the Teacher is genuinely commending enjoyment as part of a good creation, Genesis 1:31, and 1 Timothy 4:4 stands in the same line.

views.label: Joy with an accountable horizon
views.case: The book closes by joining enjoyment to judgment, 11:9 and 12:13-14. Joy is real and commended, yet not final, so it is received by someone who knows they will give account.

debates.bearing: The text itself ties enjoyment to the Giver, which separates it from escape. The third view fits the book's ending best: receive gladly, and live as someone who will stand before the One who gave.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in the chapter carry more than English shows. In verse 1 the king says he will 'test' pleasure, from the verb nasah. The same verb is used when God tests Abraham, Genesis 22:1, and Israel, Exodus 16:4. The Teacher plays God's role toward his own appetites, putting them under trial to see what they are made of. The result is a kind of failed examination in which the examiner is also the examinee.

The 'parks' of verse 5 translate pardes, a loanword from Persian that is the root of our word 'paradise.' It occurs only three times in the Old Testament: here, Song of Songs 4:13 and Nehemiah 2:8. The Septuagint renders it with the Greek word paradeisos, so a Greek reader of this verse meets the garden of Eden's later name. The Teacher is making his own paradise.

The 'reward' in verse 10 is the word cheleq, a share or portion, the same word that returns in 3:22, 5:18, 9:9 and 11:2. The Teacher's cheleq here is the pleasure of the work itself, the only share it yields. Verses 24 to 26 then redefine what a true portion is, as something from God's hand, mi-yad ha-elohim, literally 'from the hand of God.' The same word 'hand' runs through the chapter: 'the works that my hands had accomplished,' verse 11, against the hand that gives, verse 24.

Verse 14 introduces miqreh, 'fate' or 'what befalls,' from a verb that means to meet or to happen. It returns three times in 3:19 and again in 9:2-3. It is neutral on who is behind the event, and that neutrality is the Teacher's point. The wise man and the fool, the kesil, meet the same event. The kesil is the dull and stubborn fool who gets constant attention in Proverbs and who reappears in the worship warnings of 5:1-4.

Verse 19 says the heir 'will take over' the labor, from shalat, to have mastery or rule. The one who toiled with wisdom is ruled out of ownership; a stranger gains the control.

In verse 26 the one who is 'pleasing in His sight' is literally 'good before Him,' tov lefanav, and the 'sinner' is the chote', one who misses the mark. The verse is a moral contrast in the Teacher's vocabulary of the wise and the foolish, not a technical doctrine of grace.

Verse 25 carries a textual note in the BSB: 'apart from Him' follows some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint and the Syriac, while most Hebrew manuscripts read 'apart from me' or 'more than I.' The reading 'apart from Him' keeps the verse fixed on God as the source of enjoyment, while the other reading makes it a boast of the king; either way the chapter's turn stands.

Finally, the Septuagint's regular choice of mataiotes for hevel is what Paul picks up in Romans 8:20, tying Ecclesiastes' futility to the creation's subjection under the fall.

typology.type: The gardener-king who gathers the world, Ecclesiastes 2:4-9
typology.fulfillment: Solomon plants gardens, commands provinces and fills his house with the treasure of kings, and in the telling he is a new Adam in a self-made Eden, Genesis 2:8-15. He is also the son of David who has everything the devil later offers Jesus in the wilderness, 'all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,' Matthew 4:8-9. Jesus refuses the shortcut and worships the Father alone. The escalation lies there: where Solomon gathered and grew hollow, Christ refuses the counterfeit and is given the nations as His inheritance. The type falls short because Solomon's kingdom could not remove the curse of toil, while Christ's reign will end death itself, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26.

typology.type: The heir who receives what another labored for, Ecclesiastes 2:18-21
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher grieves that a stranger will enjoy what he worked for. The Bible turns the same shape the other way in the gospel. Christ is the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, and the One who labored to the cross receives nothing for Himself; those who did not work for it are made co-heirs, 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17. What was a great evil in verse 21 becomes grace. The inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4, which is the opposite of what the Teacher holds. The type breaks down because the Teacher's heir may be a fool; Christ's heirs are secured by His life.

typology.type: Food and drink from God's hand, Ecclesiastes 2:24-25
typology.fulfillment: The book's first note of joy is a table set by God. That table grows richer in the Gospels. Jesus calls Himself 'the bread of life,' John 6:35, and at the last supper gives bread and cup as His body and the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:19-20. Isaiah had asked why people spend labor 'on that which does not satisfy' when God invites them to eat what is good, Isaiah 55:2. In the supper, a gift of God's hand and a proclamation of the Lord's death meet, 1 Corinthians 11:26. The type falls short of Christ in that Ecclesiastes' meal feeds the body for a day, while this meal proclaims a death that gives life until He comes.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by contrast first. The Teacher is a son of David with unmatched wisdom and wealth, and by his own testimony it did not save him. Jesus, in Matthew 12:42, says 'One greater than Solomon is here.' The greatness is not more wealth or a longer list of projects. It is that this King does not need to gather anything to be full, and that He gives Himself away. Where the Teacher's last act is to leave everything behind, Christ's last act is to lay down His life, and the Father's answer is resurrection.

It leads to Christ by the problem the chapter cannot solve. The Teacher meets death as the great leveler of wise and foolish, verse 16. Hebrews 2:14-15 says Christ shared our flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those held in slavery by fear of it. Paul answers the Teacher's despair at the wall of mortality by saying Christ has been raised as the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and that therefore 'your labor in the Lord is not in vain,' 15:58. That last phrase is the direct reply to verse 22's question, 'what does a man get for all the toil?'

It leads to Christ by the question of treasure. The Teacher can fill a house with silver and gold and has no way to keep it. Jesus tells His followers to store up treasure in heaven where thieves do not approach and moths do not destroy, Luke 12:33-34, and promises that the heart goes where the treasure is. Paul's whole account of his own gains is the Teacher's experiment in a converted man: whatever was gain he counts as loss compared to knowing Christ, Philippians 3:7-8. Colossians 2:3 says that in Christ 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' so the wisdom the Teacher found could not guard him from death is found whole in a Person.

Finally, it leads to Christ by the gift of joy. The Teacher says joy comes from God's hand. In the Gospel of John, the Son speaks so that His joy may be in His own, John 15:11, and the Lord's Supper makes Him the one who hands over the bread. The danger is to flatten this into a simple allegory in which every meal in Ecclesiastes is the sacrament. It is better to say that the Teacher's insight about gift and giver finds its full shape in the One through whom, and for whom, all things were made, who is also the One who feeds us.
study.god:
This chapter shows God mostly by absence and then by a sudden presence. For twenty-three verses the Teacher speaks as if the world ran without a Giver, and the result is exhaustion. That absence is itself theological: it shows what life looks like when God is treated as an optional extra. When God finally appears in verse 24, He appears as the one who gives, and He is the one who determines whether a person can enjoy anything at all, 'apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?'

The passage holds together two things that people often split. God is generous: He gives food, drink, work, wisdom, knowledge and joy, and nothing in the text treats these as unholy. God is also sovereign over the distribution. The gift is not owed, and it cannot be extracted by effort. James 1:17 states the same truth: every good and perfect gift comes from above. A believer is therefore freed from two errors, the idea that pleasure is suspect and the idea that pleasure is earned.

The chapter also shows God as one who judges what is done with the gift. The 'pleasing in His sight' and 'sinner' contrast in verse 26 does not turn on wealth. It turns on whether a person is oriented to God, and Proverbs 3:13-18 and Psalm 16:11 put the same thought in positive form: wisdom and joy are found in His presence.

It shapes worship in a practical way. If every meal and every day's work comes from His hand, then thanks is the natural form of life, and Paul can write that whether we eat or drink we do it all to the glory of God, 1 Corinthians 10:31. Prayer before a meal, Sabbath rest and honest work done for the Lord, Colossians 3:23-24, are not decorations on a secular life; they are the recognition that the life is a gift.

Finally the chapter leaves a tension in place that the rest of the Bible will address: God gives joy, and yet God also lets the king see death, inheritance and toil as heavy. Romans 8:20 says it was God who subjected creation to futility, in hope. The Teacher does not resolve this. He puts both facts in front of us, and the gospel tells us how God keeps His hope.

crossReferences.note: God promised Solomon wisdom and, unasked, riches and honor beyond any king. The Teacher's claim to have surpassed all in Jerusalem rests on that gift, which sharpens the irony: even the best-gifted man cannot make gifts yield lasting profit by his own effort.

The law of the king forbids multiplying horses, wives, silver and gold. Ecclesiastes 2:8 lists silver, gold and many concubines. The experiment is unwittingly a record of breaking the law that was meant to guard the king's heart.
The ground is cursed so that toil marks every day of life. The Teacher's sleepless labor in verses 22 and 23 is this curse experienced from the inside, and no royal garden he plants can reverse it.

The rich man carries nothing away when he dies, and without understanding he is like the beasts that perish. It is the same insight as verse 16, but the psalm adds that God will redeem the writer's life from Sheol, which the Teacher does not yet say.

Without the LORD, builders and watchmen labor in vain, and early risers eat the bread of anxious toil, yet the LORD gives sleep to His beloved. It answers the sleeplessness of verse 23 with a promise of rest as a gift.

The later passage develops verses 24 to 26: enjoyment of food and labor is a lot given by God, who keeps a person occupied with the joy of the heart. The joy is not an escape from time but a way of receiving it.

Jesus tells of a man who plans bigger barns and is told his life is required that night, 'then who will own what you have accumulated?' It is verse 18's question with a face and a name, and Jesus adds that the cure is to be 'rich toward God.'

Paul says creation was subjected to futility by God 'in hope' of freedom. This gives the Teacher's word for the world its theological backing and its ending, since futility is a stage and not the final word.
Paul had a résumé like a small kingdom and counts it loss for knowing Christ. It is the converted version of the Teacher's audit, with a different conclusion because the object of desire has changed.

Paul warns that the love of money pierces people with many sorrows and also says God richly provides all things to enjoy. Both halves are present in the Teacher's chapter: grasping is a ruinous craving, and receiving is a gift.
Because Christ is raised, the labor done in the Lord is not in vain. It answers verse 22's question about what a man gets from toil: not profit under the sun, but a work that death cannot cancel.

study.oneStory:
Ecclesiastes 2 asks the question Genesis 3 left hanging. After the fall, the ground is cursed, work becomes toil and death closes the story of every life. The Teacher is a man who tries to answer that curse with every resource a person could muster, and he shows that nothing in creation can undo what was done at the beginning. His garden is a copy of Eden, and it has no tree of life.

The chapter therefore sits in the middle of the Bible's long argument about where life and rest come from. Psalm 127 says it comes from the LORD, not from early rising. Isaiah 55:2 calls the weary to stop spending money on what is not bread. Jesus calls the weary and burdened to come to Him and promises rest, Matthew 11:28. The Teacher's honest despair is the questioning that makes those promises welcome.

Its other thread is the gift. The Bible's account of creation begins with God giving: a garden, food from every tree, a helper, a day of rest. The Teacher's late discovery in verses 24 to 26 is that this original posture of receiving has not been cancelled. God still gives bread, work and joy, even to people living outside the garden.

It also looks ahead to a deliverance of work itself. Isaiah 65:21-23 pictures a people who build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and 'will not labor in vain.' Revelation 14:13 says that those who die in the Lord rest from their labors, and 'their deeds will follow them.' What the Teacher fears, that his deeds will be left to a stranger, is turned around: for those in Christ the labor goes with them.

The story ends in Revelation 21:1-5, where God dwells with His people and makes all things new, with no more death, mourning or pain. Futility is lifted, and the toil that began in Genesis 3 is finished. The tree of life stands again beside the river. In the meantime the people of God live as the Teacher counsels in his best moments: thankful for bread and work, holding wealth loosely, and waiting for the day when the labor is no longer in vain.

quiz.q: What is the Teacher doing across chapter two?

options.text: Running a controlled experiment, testing pleasure, achievement, wisdom, and toil to see if any can satisfy.
options.note: He uses his royal resources to test every avenue while keeping his wisdom to judge the results.

options.text: Indulging recklessly in wine, wealth, and pleasure with no restraint.
options.note: He explicitly keeps his wisdom throughout; it is a deliberate test, not a blind binge.

options.text: Recording the history of his building projects for posterity.
options.note: He does catalogue his works, but as evidence in an experiment about what satisfies, not as mere history.

options.text: Teaching that all pleasure and work are sinful.
options.note: He ends by receiving food, work, and joy as good gifts from God's hand.

quiz.q: Why does the Teacher call even his greatest achievements futile?

options.text: Death levels the wise and the fool, and everything he built must be left to someone else.
options.note: Loss and death undo every human gain under the sun, so nothing lasts as ultimate profit.

options.text: Because he had to hand his life's work to an heir who might be a fool.
options.note: True and part of it, though the deeper leveler is death itself, which takes wise and fool alike.

options.text: Because his projects failed and his wealth ran out.
options.note: His works succeeded gloriously; that is what makes the emptiness so striking.

options.text: Because God was punishing him for building too much.
options.note: The issue is the limits of life under the sun, not divine punishment for his projects.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the turn in verses 24 to 26?

options.text: For the first time the Teacher looks up to God, receiving food, work, and joy as gifts from His hand.
options.note: The chapter turns from grasping under the sun to receiving daily good from God the giver.

options.text: He concludes that simple everyday joys are the good God gives.
options.note: A faithful summary, though it understates that the key is naming God as the giver for the first time.

options.text: He decides that pleasure was worth pursuing after all.
options.note: The point is not that grasping pleasure works, but that ordinary joys are received as gifts, not wages.

options.text: He gives up on God and settles for eating and drinking.
options.note: The turn is toward God as giver, not away from Him into resignation.

quiz.q: How does the phrase eat and drink and enjoy your work function here?

options.text: As grace: ordinary joys received from God's hand, not seized as wages or worshiped as gods.
options.note: The good of daily life is a gift to be received, which reframes pleasure rightly.

options.text: As permission to enjoy the simple gifts of everyday life gratefully.
options.note: True, and the crucial addition is that these come from the hand of God as gifts.

options.text: As a call to lower your expectations and just get by.
options.note: It is not grim resignation but glad reception of God's daily gifts.

options.text: As a command to pursue as much pleasure as possible.
options.note: The Teacher has just shown that grasping for pleasure fails; this is receiving, not seizing.

quiz.q: How does chapter two point forward to Christ?

options.text: As a son of David who gains the world yet cannot keep it, he sets off Christ, the greater than Solomon who secures an inheritance that death cannot take.
options.note: Solomon's emptiness magnifies the Son of David who makes even our fleeting labor last.

options.text: It dramatizes Jesus question about gaining the world and losing the soul.
options.note: True, Mark 8:36, though the fuller point is Christ securing what Solomon could not keep.

options.text: It proves that wealthy people cannot be saved.
options.note: The lesson is about the limits of gaining the world, not a verdict that the rich cannot be saved.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ or the wider Bible.
options.note: It connects directly to Jesus as the greater than Solomon and to labor not in vain in the Lord.

questions: The Teacher tested pleasure to its limit and found it empty. Where are you hoping that one more experience, purchase, or achievement will finally satisfy you?
He built impressive things and still had to leave them all behind. What are you pouring your life into that you cannot ultimately keep, and how does that reshape how you hold it?
Death levels the wise and the fool alike in this chapter. How does facing that honestly change what you want your fleeting days to count for?
The turning point is receiving food, work, and joy as gifts from God's hand rather than seizing them as wages. Where do you need to move from grasping to gratefully receiving?
Jesus is the greater than Solomon who makes our labor not in vain. How does knowing that your work in the Lord lasts forever change the way you approach an ordinary week?

translationNotes.note: Futile is hevel, a breath or vapor. The pleasure is not condemned as evil but weighed and found unable to satisfy or endure, slipping away like mist.
A pursuit of the wind renders the idiom for chasing the ruach, the wind, and there was nothing to be gained translates the loss of yitron, any lasting profit, under the sun.
The recommendation to eat and drink and enjoy one's work is not resignation but the first turn to God as giver: these are gifts from the hand of God, received rather than seized.
